414.title: Kedoshim: as yourself (Leviticus 19:18)
414.hook: "thou shalt love thy neighbor as thyself"; Rabbi Akiva called it the great principle of the Torah
414.howItsDone: Some prayer books open the morning service with a line taking on the commandment of loving one's neighbor as oneself, a custom traced to the kabbalist Isaac Luria, and Hillel's summary is often taught in Jewish schools.

segments.voice: Yesterday in Kedoshim, a verse that won't let us just watch. Your line was don't stand idly by. Did you step in somewhere? Today, two verses later, a line that has traveled far beyond the chapter. Day four hundred fourteen.

This line turns up on posters, at weddings, in speeches, on bumper stickers. Words that familiar can slide right off. But it's only the second half of a verse. The first half rarely makes it onto the poster, and it changes how the famous part sounds. It's not about warm feelings for nice people. It's about the person who did harm last month, and the grudge that's been quietly kept ever since.
screen: `ON POSTERS AND BUMPER STICKERS.` → `THE HALF THAT COMES FIRST.` → `THE ONE WHO WRONGED YOU.`

segments.voice: First, the whole verse. In the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: "Thou shalt not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge against the children of thy people, but thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself: I am the LORD." The love comes right after the grudge. It's the alternative to revenge. Second, the knife. The Jerusalem Talmud explains vengeance with a picture. Someone is cutting meat, and the knife slips and cuts their hand. Would the cut hand turn around and stab the hand that held the knife? Of course not. They're one body. So, too, the people: hurting each other back is like a body attacking itself. Third, Rabbi Akiva. He called this verse a great principle of the Torah, klal gadol. His colleague Ben Azzai named a different verse as greater still: the line in Genesis about the generations of Adam, the human being made in God's likeness. Love your neighbor might depend on how you feel about yourself, some explain. Ben Azzai's verse grounds it in every person's dignity. The two teachings sit side by side in the sources. Fourth, how it's lived. When a man asked Hillel to teach him the whole Torah while standing on one foot, Hillel said: what is hateful to you, don't do to your neighbor. That is the whole Torah; the rest is commentary. Now go and learn. As yourself: a measure every person carries.
screen: `NO VENGEANCE, NO GRUDGE.` · `ONE BODY: THE CUT HAND.` · `AKIVA: THE GREAT PRINCIPLE.` · `HILLEL ON ONE FOOT.` · then, large: `AS YOURSELF.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do one loving thing for a neighbor. Settle, and breathe. Think of a neighbor, literal or not: the person next door, at the next desk, in the next seat. Maybe even one you've got a small grudge against. Ask what you'd want if you were them today. A hand with groceries, a kind word, a returned favor, an apology accepted. Choose one thing, and picture doing it. The bell holds the time.
Kedoshim. The portion with love thy neighbor as thyself, which Rabbi Akiva called the great principle of the Torah, set right after the ban on grudges.
Your line: as yourself. Today, before you act toward someone, ask what you'd want in their place, and do that. Day four hundred fourteen.

415.title: Emor: say it twice (Leviticus 21:1)
415.hook: "speak" and "say" are doubled; Rashi reads it as elders teaching the young
415.howItsDone: Jewish tradition treats teaching the next generation as a commandment, from the Shema's command to teach these words to one's children, and the Passover seder is built around children's questions and adults' answers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kedoshim ended with love thy neighbor. Your line was as yourself. Did you treat someone the way you'd want to be treated? Today, a new portion, and a word that appears twice. Day four hundred fifteen.

Look both ways. Say thank you. Call your grandmother. Some phrases get said in a family so often they wear a groove. A child groans at them. Then, years later, the same words come out of that child's mouth, to a kid of their own, or a niece, or a new hire at work. The next portion of Leviticus is named Emor, say. And its first verse has a small oddity that a careful reader can't miss: God tells Moses to speak to the priests, and then, in the same breath, to say to them. Why both?
screen: `LOOK BOTH WAYS. SAY THANK YOU.` → `THE WORDS COME BACK.` → `SPEAK, AND SAY.`

segments.voice: First, the verse. In the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: "Speak unto the priests the sons of Aaron, and say unto them". In Hebrew, emor, say, and then ve-amarta, and you shall say. Two forms of the same verb, one right after the other. Second, a rabbinic principle: the Torah doesn't waste words. If something seems repeated, it's there to teach something more. Third, Rashi's reading. Rashi, drawing on the Talmud, says the doubling is there to charge the adults regarding the young. The law that follows is about priests keeping away from contact with the dead, except for close family. The grown priests are told: it isn't enough to keep this yourselves. You're responsible for your children keeping it too. One say for you, one say for them. Fourth, the wider teaching. Later teachers take Rashi's reading further. Every generation says it twice: once by doing it, and once by teaching it. A practice that isn't passed on lasts exactly one lifetime. The Shema says it too: teach these words diligently to your children. And notice how Rashi phrases it. The adults are warned about the young. The responsibility runs downhill, from the ones who know to the ones still learning. Whatever you've learned on this path, someone around you hasn't heard it yet.
screen: `EMOR, VE-AMARTA: SAY, AND SAY.` · `THE TORAH DOESN'T WASTE WORDS.` · `RASHI: THE ADULTS, FOR THE YOUNG.` · `SAID ONCE BY DOING, ONCE BY TEACHING.` · then, large: `THE OLD TEACH THE YOUNG.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: teach one small thing. Settle, and breathe. Think back over what you've picked up in these four hundred days, or anywhere else in your life. A word, a story, a habit, a skill. Now think of someone younger than you, or newer, who might like to know it. A child, a niece, a colleague, a friend just starting out. Pick one small thing, and imagine how you'd say it in a sentence or two. The bell holds the time.
Emor. Say: the portion that opens with speak and say doubled, which Rashi reads as the adults' charge for the young.
Your line: the old teach the young. Today, pass on one small thing you know to someone who doesn't know it yet. Day four hundred fifteen.

416.title: Emor: appointed times (Leviticus 23)
416.hook: Shabbat, Passover, the Omer, Shavuot, the new year, Yom Kippur, Sukkot, all in one chapter
416.howItsDone: The Jewish calendar follows Leviticus 23's festivals on a lunar-solar year fixed by rabbinic calculation; Leviticus 22–23 is read in synagogue on several festivals, and some Jewish homes keep a Hebrew calendar beside the ordinary one.

segments.voice: Yesterday in Emor, speak and say, doubled. Your line was the old teach the young. Did you pass one small thing on? Today, the chapter that builds the Jewish year. Day four hundred sixteen.

Open a Jewish calendar and you'll see two systems at once. The ordinary months, January, February. And, printed smaller, Hebrew months with names like Nisan and Tishrei, and holidays that wander across the ordinary calendar from year to year. Ask where that second calendar comes from, and much of the answer is one chapter. Leviticus 23 lays out the sacred year from beginning to end, in forty-four verses. The great festivals a Jewish family keeps today have their roots here; Hanukkah and Purim came later.
screen: `TWO CALENDARS AT ONCE.` → `HOLIDAYS THAT WANDER.` → `ONE CHAPTER, FORTY-FOUR VERSES.`

segments.voice: First, the word. The chapter opens, in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: "The appointed seasons of the LORD, which ye shall proclaim to be holy convocations". In Hebrew, mo'adim. A mo'ed is a set time, an appointment. The Tent of Meeting, where God meets Moses, is the ohel mo'ed: same root. A holiday, in this picture, is a date God keeps with the people. Second, the list. Shabbat comes first, every seventh day. Then Passover and the week of matzah in spring. The first sheaf of barley, the omer, and seven weeks counted to Shavuot. Then the seventh month: a day of blowing the horn, which became Rosh Hashanah; Yom Kippur on the tenth; and Sukkot, the festival of booths, on the fifteenth. Third, who sets the date. The verse says these are the times ye shall proclaim. The Talmud tells of a dispute over when a month began, and reads the word for them, otam, as if it said atem, you: the people's court fixes the calendar, even if it errs. God's appointments, the rabbis taught, are kept on the people's calendar. Fourth, the rhythm. The year in Leviticus 23 isn't a list of days off. Spring is freedom, early summer is gift, fall is judgment, forgiveness and joy. It gives time a shape, so a year isn't one long run of the same day. Appointed times.
screen: `MO'ED: AN APPOINTMENT.` · `SHABBAT, SPRING, SUMMER, FALL.` · `ATEM: YOU SET THE DATE.` · `TIME GIVEN A SHAPE.` · then, large: `APPOINTED TIMES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: mark the next holiday on your calendar. Settle, and breathe. Think about your year. Which days stand out, and which blur together? Now think of the next holiday that matters to you, whatever it is: a Jewish festival, a family day, an anniversary. After the bell, put it on your calendar, and add one thing you'll do to keep the appointment: a meal, a call, a candle, a walk. The bell holds the time.
Mo'adim. Appointed times: the sacred calendar of Leviticus 23, from Shabbat through Passover, Shavuot, the new year, Yom Kippur and Sukkot.
Your line: appointed times. Today, put one appointment with something that matters into your calendar, and treat it like a meeting you can't miss. Day four hundred sixteen.

417.title: Emor: counting fifty days (Leviticus 23:15–16)
417.hook: from barley harvest to wheat, seven weeks counted day by day
417.howItsDone: From the second night of Passover until Shavuot, many Jews count the omer each evening after nightfall, saying a blessing and the day's number in days and weeks; some keep a counting chart or app at home.

segments.voice: Yesterday in Emor, mo'adim, the appointed times. Your line was appointed times. Did one appointment make it onto your calendar? Today, the stretch between two of them, counted one day at a time. Day four hundred seventeen.

Kids know how to count toward something. Twelve more sleeps until my birthday. Eleven. Ten. Adults do it too, more quietly: days sober, days until the wedding, days since the diagnosis, days until the baby is due. The counting doesn't make the day come faster. It changes what the days in between feel like. They stop being empty. They become the way there. Leviticus 23 builds that kind of countdown into the year, and the counting itself becomes the practice.
screen: `TWELVE MORE SLEEPS.` → `THE DAYS IN BETWEEN.` → `A HOLIDAY KEPT BY COUNTING.`

segments.voice: First, the instruction. After Passover, the people bring the omer, the first sheaf of the harvest; barley, in the rabbis' reading. From that day they count. In the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: "seven weeks shall there be complete". Fifty days, and on the fiftieth, Shavuot, the festival of weeks, with two loaves of bread from the new grain. In the rabbis' reading, barley to wheat. Second, when to start. The verse says to count from the morrow after the sabbath. Which sabbath? The rabbis read it as the first day of Passover, so the count begins on the second night. Other groups in ancient times, the Boethusians, read it as the Saturday after Passover. The Talmud records a long argument. Rabbinic practice follows the rabbis' count. Third, how it's done. Each night, after dark, the custom is to say a blessing and then the number: today is one day of the omer. Later: today is twenty-three days, which is three weeks and two days. Day by day, and week by week. Miss a whole day, and the Shulchan Aruch rules you keep counting, but without the blessing. Fourth, what the counting means. The rabbis linked Shavuot to the giving of the Torah at Sinai, so the count became a walk from freedom to purpose: out of Egypt, toward the mountain. This path counts its days too. Today is four hundred seventeen.
screen: `THE OMER: THE FIRST SHEAF.` · `THE MORROW AFTER WHICH SABBATH?` · `TODAY IS ONE DAY OF THE OMER.` · `FROM FREEDOM TO SINAI.` · then, large: `COUNT TOWARD SOMETHING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: count one day toward something. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you're moving toward. A goal, a change, a reunion, a recovery, a date on the calendar. How many days away is it, roughly? Now, in your head, say it the way the omer is counted: today is one day. Just one. Not the whole distance. Let today be a step, instead of a wait. The bell holds the time.
Emor. The portion that commands counting seven weeks, from the first sheaf after Passover to the new bread of Shavuot, day by day.
Your line: count toward something. Tonight, write down day one of something you're moving toward, and count tomorrow too. Day four hundred seventeen.

418.title: Emor: the poor at the feast (Leviticus 23:22)
418.hook: in the middle of the festivals, a reminder to leave gleanings for the poor
418.howItsDone: Jewish festivals include giving: the Passover seder's telling opens with an invitation to the hungry, Purim includes matanot la'evyonim, gifts to the poor, and some families give tzedakah before Shabbat and holidays.

segments.voice: Yesterday in Emor, fifty days counted from barley to wheat. Your line was count toward something. Did you write down day one? Today, a verse that interrupts the festival calendar. Day four hundred eighteen.

A holiday table. The good dishes, the long tablecloth, too much food, cousins arguing about seating. It's the best kind of chaos. And somewhere in the same city, at the same hour, someone is eating alone, or not eating much at all. Leviticus 23 has been walking through the festivals in order: Passover, the omer, Shavuot. The next thing should be the seventh month, the new year. But right there, in between, the Torah stops the calendar for one verse that isn't about a festival at all.
screen: `THE GOOD DISHES, TOO MUCH FOOD.` → `SOMEONE EATING ALONE.` → `ONE VERSE IN BETWEEN.`

segments.voice: First, the verse. Right after Shavuot, the harvest feast, in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: when you reap your field, don't reap its corner fully, or gather the gleanings, "thou shalt leave them for the poor, and for the stranger: I am the LORD your God." You've heard almost the same words before, in Kedoshim, a week ago. So why say it again, here? Second, Rashi's answer. He cites a rabbi named Avdimi, who asks exactly that: why put the gifts for the poor in the middle of the festivals? To teach that whoever leaves the gleanings and the corner properly is considered as if they had built the Temple and brought offerings in it. Feeding the poor sits in the same list as the holiest days, and counts like an offering. Third, Maimonides on joy. He rules that when you eat and drink on a festival, you must also feed the stranger, the orphan, the widow, and others in need. And he's blunt: someone who locks their doors and feasts only with their own family isn't celebrating a commandment. That, he says, is the joy of their stomach. Fourth, how it's lived. Early in the Passover seder, well before the meal, the table hears the words: let all who are hungry come and eat. On Purim, gifts to the poor are part of the day itself. A Jewish feast is supposed to have an open edge, like a field with its corners left uncut.
screen: `THE HARVEST VERSE, AGAIN.` · `RASHI: AS IF YOU BUILT THE TEMPLE.` · `NOT THE JOY OF THE STOMACH.` · `LET ALL WHO ARE HUNGRY COME.` · then, large: `REMEMBER THEM AT THE FEAST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give during a celebration. Settle, and breathe. Think of the next celebration on your calendar: a holiday, a birthday, a dinner out, even a good weekend. Picture the table. Now picture an empty chair at it. Who could that chair be for? A neighbor alone for the holiday, a student far from home, a food bank, a gift in someone's name. Choose one way you'll give as part of the celebration, not after it. The bell holds the time.
Emor. The portion that pauses its calendar of feasts to remind the reapers to leave something for the poor and the stranger.
Your line: remember them at the feast. The next time you celebrate, give something away as part of the party. Day four hundred eighteen.

419.title: Emor: one law (Leviticus 24:22)
419.hook: "Ye shall have one manner of law, as well for the stranger, as for the home-born"
419.howItsDone: Jewish law and teaching repeatedly cite the Torah's command not to wrong the ger, the stranger, and the Passover seder's memory of being strangers in Egypt is often linked to welcoming outsiders.

segments.voice: Yesterday in Emor, the poor were remembered at the feast. Your line was remember them at the feast. Did you plan a gift into a celebration? Today, the end of Emor, and a story about an outsider. Day four hundred nineteen.

Near the end of Emor, the long list of laws suddenly breaks into a story. A fight in the camp. One of the men has an Israelite mother, Shelomith, daughter of Dibri, from the tribe of Dan, and an Egyptian father. In the quarrel, he curses the Name of God. Nobody is sure what to do with him. Half-insider, half-outsider. Does the law even apply to someone like that? They put him in custody and wait for an answer.
screen: `A FIGHT IN THE CAMP.` → `AN ISRAELITE MOTHER, AN EGYPTIAN FATHER.` → `DOES THE LAW APPLY TO HIM?`

segments.voice: The verdict comes, and it's severe, as the Torah's punishments for cursing God are. But then the text widens from this one man to everyone, and lays down laws about harming people and animals. In the middle of them is a sentence that answers the question that started it all. In the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: "Ye shall have one manner of law, as well for the stranger, as for the home-born; for I am the LORD your God." The Hebrew word for stranger is ger, someone living among the people who wasn't born into them. The same law protects them and binds them. No special harshness for the outsider, and no special leniency for the insider. It isn't the first time the Torah has said this. At the very first Passover, in Exodus, it already set down one law for the home-born and for the stranger who lives among you. Now, at a moment of real doubt, it says it again. And the hard verse nearby gets the same treatment. This same passage has the line people quote as an eye for an eye. The rabbis of the Talmud ruled that it means payment: the value of an eye, not an actual eye, and they argued for it at length. Rabbinic law followed that ruling, and applied it, for the same injury, to everyone. One measure, for the ger and the home-born alike. It started with a man nobody was sure about.
screen: `A STORY BREAKS INTO THE LAWS.` · `GER: THE ONE WHO LIVES AMONG YOU.` · `ONE LAW SINCE THE FIRST PASSOVER.` · `AN EYE MEANS ITS VALUE.` · then, large: `ONE LAW FOR ALL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: treat an outsider as an equal. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone who's a stranger in a place you know well. The new person at work. The neighbor with an accent. The family that moved in last month. The person at the edge of your group chat. Notice whether you hold them to a different standard, stricter or more dismissive, than the people you grew up with. Picture treating them by exactly the same rules as everyone else. The bell holds the time.
Emor. The portion that ends with one law for the stranger and the home-born alike.
Your line: one law for all. Today, catch yourself if you judge a newcomer by a harder rule, and use the same one you'd use for a friend. Day four hundred nineteen.

420.title: Behar: the land rests (Leviticus 25:1–7)
420.hook: every seventh year the land lies fallow and its produce is open to all
420.howItsDone: In Israel the shmita year is observed by some farmers and consumers, through fallowing, special arrangements for produce, or a contested legal sale of land; outside Israel, Jews study its laws and some communities mark the year with learning and giving.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Emor ended with one law for the stranger and the home-born. Your line was one law for all. Did you use the same rule for a newcomer? Today, a new portion, and a Sabbath for the soil. Day four hundred twenty.

Here is the instruction to a farmer: for one whole year out of every seven, don't sow. Don't prune the vines. Don't harvest the way you normally would. Whatever grows by itself becomes food for everyone, including the hired workers, the settler, and even the wild animals. On paper, it sounds like a recipe for hunger. In modern Israel, farmers and rabbis still wrestle over how to keep it. And the Torah opens the portion with a strange address: it says this was spoken at Mount Sinai.
screen: `ONE YEAR IN SEVEN: DON'T PLANT.` → `ANYONE MAY TAKE.` → `SPOKEN AT MOUNT SINAI.`

segments.voice: First, the law. When you come into the land, in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation, "then shall the land keep a sabbath unto the LORD." Six years you sow and harvest. The seventh is the year tradition calls shmita, a release. The land lies fallow. Second, who eats. What grows on its own is for everyone: you, your servants, your hired worker, the settler living with you, your cattle, and the wild animals in your land. For a year, the owner's fence means less. The rich farmer and the poor stranger eat from the same field. Third, why Sinai? Rashi asks: what does the sabbatical year have to do with Mount Sinai? Weren't all the commandments given at Sinai? His answer: just as shmita was given with its general rules and its fine details at Sinai, so were all the others. Fourth, the week behind us. As yourself closed Kedoshim. Emor said it twice, set the appointed times, counted fifty days, fed the poor at the feast, and gave one law for all. Now Behar, on the mountain, lets the ground rest. Shmita is still observed in Israel, in different ways in different communities. In other places, people borrow its rhythm: a sabbatical, a fallow season, a year of letting something lie.
